description:
ARES Health AI is a remote, Spanish-speaking team developing a prototype to help astronauts monitor health indicators and identify potential risks during long-duration missions.

I'm a student from Mexico with experience in personal AI projects and Python. We welcome motivated teammates in software development, data analysis, AI/ML, UX/UI, and biomedical research.

All experience levels are welcome. Our goal is to build a practical, evidence-informed solution through collaboration.
summary:
ARES Health AI, which stands for Astronaut Risk Evaluation System, represents a suggested tool intended to function without constant internet access for tracking crew wellness and aiding choices during extended trips beyond Earth orbit.

Astronauts face physiological and psychological hurdles within space settings, such as heart function shifts, disrupted rest patterns, and extended solitude.

This proposed system intends to merge physiological markers with user-submitted wellness data within a reachable interface. By applying Python tools, statistical evaluation, and transparent anomaly-finding techniques, ARES will spot atypical shifts in personal health patterns and deliver clear notifications.

At first, the prototype shall employ simulated physiological inputs alongside repeatable test conditions to show how it works. Its goal is to aid in building health knowledge and making educated choices, rather than taking over from doctors or their expert opinions.

The aim here involves investigating just how usable, proof-based computer programs might boost crew independence and wellness tracking throughout upcoming space travel endeavors.
details:
ARES Health AI: Astronaut Risk Evaluation System

What is ARES?

ARES is a prototype I built to explore a simple question: how could astronauts keep track of their own wellness on a long mission when contact with Earth is slow or cut off completely? It works offline, shows its reasoning, and leaves every decision to a person.

How it works

Monitoring. ARES charts three synthetic indicators: resting heart rate, sleep duration, and daily physical activity. You can explore the charts and see how each one changes over time.

Validation and analysis. A Python engine first checks that the data is complete and consistent. Then it compares a reference period against a recent one, and flags changes that cross illustrative thresholds for fictional review. If records are missing or don't add up, ARES doesn't interpret the trend at all. It tells you why instead of guessing.

ARES Copilot. The Copilot is rule-based and runs offline. It explains what changed, shows the measurements behind it, and points out what it can't tell you. It is not a generative model, and it doesn't diagnose or recommend treatment.

Wellness and human review. Short educational modules connect the readings to public NASA Human Research Program literature. Users can log fictional review actions, follow a mission timeline, and export a structured JSON report.

Offline use. ARES runs locally on a prepared Windows setup with React and FastAPI, no internet needed. I tested the core workflows with the connection turned off. A separate public demo is hosted online so anyone can try it.

How it was built

I used Python, FastAPI, React, TypeScript, Vite, Recharts, Docker, and GitHub Actions. Validation, analysis, explanations, and the interface are kept in separate layers, and the synthetic data is generated reproducibly with Python. Testing covers the backend, frontend, HTTP, and browser, plus manual runs both online and offline.

Why it matters

ARES doesn't try to be a medical prediction tool. What it offers is the combination of a few ideas in one prototype:

  • It keeps working when communication drops.
  • Every result can be traced back to the measurements behind it.
  • It refuses to interpret data that can't support a conclusion.
  • A person stays in control, with a JSON record of what was reviewed.
  • It gives accessible scientific context about human spaceflight.

A natural next step would be to test these ideas with authorized datasets, protocols reviewed by specialists, and controlled studies.

Limitations

  • ARES uses synthetic data, not real astronaut records.
  • The thresholds are illustrative engineering values, not clinically validated limits or NASA standards.
  • It doesn't diagnose, prescribe, or authorize medical decisions, and it doesn't replace flight surgeons or approved procedures.
  • NASA publications are used only as references. ARES is an independent project and is not endorsed, certified, or operated by NASA.

Public demo: https://ares-health-ai.onrender.com
